clinicalPearls: Caused by biallelic CAPN3 variants; calpainopathy is the most common form of limb-girdle muscular dystrophy worldwide.
Classically autosomal recessive, although a dominant form due to specific CAPN3 variants is now also recognised.
Predominantly an atrophic phenotype — the absence of calf hypertrophy helps distinguish it from dystroglycanopathies and sarcoglycanopathies.
Early and selective involvement of the posterior thigh (hamstrings and adductors) and hip-girdle and gluteal muscles, with scapular winging and a scapulo-humeral pattern.
Achilles and other tendon contractures may precede overt weakness, and abdominal wall laxity can occur.
Cardiac muscle is characteristically spared, and respiratory involvement is usually late and comparatively mild.
Serum creatine kinase is elevated, often markedly so in the early symptomatic phase.
Immunoblot may show reduced calpain-3, but a normal result does not exclude the diagnosis because function can be lost with preserved protein quantity — genetic confirmation is essential.
reference.pathophysiology: CAPN3 encodes calpain-3, a skeletal-muscle-specific, calcium-dependent cysteine protease anchored to titin within the sarcomere. It participates in sarcomere remodelling, in the regulated turnover of cytoskeletal and signalling substrates, and in muscle regeneration. Loss of its proteolytic and regulatory activity disturbs sarcomere maintenance and the calcium-dependent signalling that supports myofibre adaptation, producing disorganised regeneration, myofibre atrophy and necrosis with progressive fibrofatty replacement. Because binding to titin also protects calpain-3 from autolysis, disorders of titin can cause a secondary reduction of calpain-3 on immunoblot, a recognised diagnostic trap.
additionalDifferentials: FKRP-related limb-girdle dystrophy (R9) and other dystroglycanopathies
Becker muscular dystrophy and manifesting dystrophinopathy carriers
Titinopathy (a cause of secondary calpain-3 deficiency)
additionalInvestigations: CAPN3 sequencing with deletion and duplication analysis, or a next-generation neuromuscular gene panel
Muscle biopsy showing dystrophic features, with calpain-3 immunoblot
Muscle MRI — selective posterior thigh and paraspinal involvement supports the diagnosis
Baseline cardiac and respiratory assessment to document typically preserved cardiac function and to monitor for late respiratory decline
redFlags: Rapidly progressive weakness or accelerated loss of ambulation
Late symptoms of nocturnal hypoventilation such as morning headache, daytime somnolence and orthopnoea
Falls and fracture risk arising from proximal weakness
Unexpected cardiac symptoms, which should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis because cardiac involvement is atypical
reference.prognosis: The disease is slowly progressive, with loss of independent ambulation typically occurring years to decades after onset and with wide individual variability. Cardiac sparing and generally later respiratory involvement give a comparatively favourable systemic prognosis relative to several other muscular dystrophies.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal calpain-3 immunoblot excludes the disease — enzymatic function may be lost with preserved protein, so confirm genetically.
Stopping at a reduced calpain-3 immunoblot, which can be secondary to a titinopathy rather than primary calpainopathy.
Misreading early eosinophilic infiltrates on biopsy as inflammatory myositis and initiating inappropriate immunosuppression.
Interpreting scapular winging as evidence of facioscapulohumeral dystrophy.
Discounting the diagnosis because calf hypertrophy is absent — its absence is expected here.
management: Recognise there is no disease-modifying drug and use physiotherapy, stretching and occupational therapy to maintain function and prevent Achilles and other tendon contractures
Undertake respiratory surveillance with pulmonary function testing and non-invasive ventilation for the usually late respiratory decline
Perform baseline cardiac assessment, recognising that cardiac muscle is characteristically spared
Provide orthoses and mobility aids as weakness progresses, with loss of ambulation typically only after years to decades
Provide genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance, noting a dominant form is also recognised, and screen relatives
